Let $\alpha_{1}, \alpha_{2}, \cdots, \alpha_{5}$ be five 1000-dimensional vectors, and let $\alpha_{i}(j)$ denote the $j$-th element of $\alpha_{i}$. Then $\alpha_{1}, \alpha_{2}, \cdots, \alpha_{5}$ satisfy
$$
\alpha_{i}(j)=\left\{\begin{array}{l}
1, j \in A_{i} ; \\
0, j \notin A_{i} .
\end{array}\right.
$$

Let the maximum number of common elements in any three subsets be $r$.
For any three vectors
$$
\begin{array}{l}
\boldsymbol{\beta}_{1}=\left(b_{1}, b_{2}, \cdots, b_{t}\right), \boldsymbol{\gamma}_{1}=\left(c_{1}, c_{2}, \cdots, c_{t}\right), \\
\boldsymbol{\delta}_{1}=\left(d_{1}, d_{2}, \cdots, d_{t}\right),
\end{array}
$$

define the ternary inner product operation
$$
\left(\boldsymbol{\beta}_{1}, \boldsymbol{\gamma}_{1}, \boldsymbol{\delta}_{1}\right)=b_{1} c_{1} d_{1}+b_{2} c_{2} d_{2}+\cdots+b_{t} c_{t} d_{t} .
$$

Clearly, this operation is linear and satisfies the commutative law.
By the problem, $\left(\boldsymbol{\alpha}_{i}, \boldsymbol{\alpha}_{i}, \boldsymbol{\alpha}_{i}\right)=500$.
For $1 \leqslant i<j<k \leqslant 5,\left(\boldsymbol{\alpha}_{i}, \boldsymbol{\alpha}_{j}, \boldsymbol{\alpha}_{k}\right)$ equals the number of common elements in the sets $A_{i}, A_{j}, A_{k}$.
Let $\boldsymbol{\alpha}=\boldsymbol{\alpha}_{1}+\boldsymbol{\alpha}_{2}+\boldsymbol{\alpha}_{3}+\boldsymbol{\alpha}_{4}+\boldsymbol{\alpha}_{5}$. Then
$(\boldsymbol{\alpha}, \boldsymbol{\alpha}, \boldsymbol{\alpha})$
$$
\begin{aligned}
= & \sum_{i=1}^{5}\left(\boldsymbol{\alpha}_{i}, \boldsymbol{\alpha}_{i}, \boldsymbol{\alpha}_{i}\right)+3 \sum_{i \neq j}\left(\boldsymbol{\alpha}_{i}, \boldsymbol{\alpha}_{i}, \boldsymbol{\alpha}_{j}\right)+ \\
& 6 \sum_{i<j<k}\left(\boldsymbol{\alpha}_{i}, \boldsymbol{\alpha}_{j}, \boldsymbol{\alpha}_{k}\right) \\
= & 2500+3 \sum_{i \neq j}\left(\boldsymbol{\alpha}_{i}, \boldsymbol{\alpha}_{i}, \boldsymbol{\alpha}_{j}\right)+6 \sum_{i<j<k}\left(\boldsymbol{\alpha}_{i}, \boldsymbol{\alpha}_{j}, \boldsymbol{\alpha}_{k}\right) \\
\leqslant & 2500+3 \sum_{i \neq j}\left(\boldsymbol{\alpha}_{i}, \boldsymbol{\alpha}_{i}, \boldsymbol{\alpha}_{j}\right)+60 r .
\end{aligned}
$$

Also, $\boldsymbol{\alpha}$ is a 1000-dimensional vector, and
$$
\boldsymbol{\alpha}=\left(a_{1}, a_{2}, \cdots, a_{1000}\right)\left(a_{i} \in\{0,1, \cdots, 5\}\right),
$$

satisfying $\sum_{i=1}^{1000} a_{i}=2500$.
At this point, $(\boldsymbol{\alpha}, \boldsymbol{\alpha}, \boldsymbol{\alpha})=\sum_{i=1}^{1000} a_{i}^{3}$, and $\left(\boldsymbol{\alpha}_{i}, \boldsymbol{\alpha}_{i}, \boldsymbol{\alpha}_{j}\right)$ represents the number of common elements in the sets $A_{i}$ and $A_{j}$, so $\left(\boldsymbol{\alpha}_{i}, \boldsymbol{\alpha}_{i}, \boldsymbol{\alpha}_{j}\right)=\left(\boldsymbol{\alpha}_{i}, \boldsymbol{\alpha}_{j}\right)$, where $(\boldsymbol{a}, \boldsymbol{b})$ denotes the usual inner product of vectors $\boldsymbol{a}$ and $\boldsymbol{b}$.
$$
\begin{array}{l}
\text { Hence } \sum_{i \neq j}\left(\boldsymbol{\alpha}_{i}, \boldsymbol{\alpha}_{i}, \boldsymbol{\alpha}_{j}\right)=\sum_{i \neq j}\left(\boldsymbol{\alpha}_{i}, \boldsymbol{\alpha}_{j}\right) \\
=(\boldsymbol{\alpha}, \boldsymbol{\alpha})-\sum_{i=1}^{5}\left(\boldsymbol{\alpha}_{i}, \boldsymbol{\alpha}_{i}\right) \\
=\sum_{i=1}^{1000} a_{i}^{2}-2500 .
\end{array}
$$

At this point,
$$
\begin{array}{l}
60 r \geqslant \sum_{i=1}^{1000} a_{i}^{3}-3\left(\sum_{i=1}^{1000} a_{i}^{2}-2500\right)-2500 \\
=\sum_{i=1}^{1000}\left(a_{i}^{3}-3 a_{i}^{2}\right)+5000 . \\
\text { Also, }\left(a_{i}-2\right)\left(a_{i}-3\right)\left(a_{i}+2\right) \geqslant 0 \\
\Leftrightarrow a_{i}^{3}-3 a_{i}^{2}-4 a_{i}+12 \geqslant 0 .
\end{array}
$$

Thus, for any $1 \leqslant i \leqslant 1000$,
$$
a_{i}^{3}-3 a_{i}^{2} \geqslant 4 a_{i}-12 \text {. }
$$

Therefore, $60 r \geqslant \sum_{i=1}^{1000}\left(4 a_{i}-12\right)+5000$
$$
=4 \times 2500-12000+5000=3000 \text {. }
$$

A teacher is planning to give the children a problem of the following type. He will inform them that he has thought of a polynomial $P(x)$ of degree 2017 with integer coefficients, the leading coefficient of which is 1. Then he will tell them $k$ integers $n_{1}, n_{2}, \ldots, n_{k}$ and separately inform them of the value of the expression $P\left(n_{1}\right) P\left(n_{2}\right) \ldots P\left(n_{k}\right)$. Based on this data, the children are supposed to find the polynomial that the teacher could have thought of. For what smallest $k$ can the teacher formulate such a problem so that the polynomial found by the children will definitely match the one thought of?

meta.gold_solution:
Evaluation. Let the teacher use some $k \leq 2016$, and consider the polynomial $P(x)$.

Consider the polynomial $P(x)=P(x)+\left(x-n_{1}\right)\left(x-n_{2}\right) \ldots\left(x-n_{k}\right)$. Notice that the degree of the polynomial $Q(x)$ is also

2017, and its leading coefficient is also 1. Moreover, $P\left(n_{1}\right) P\left(n_{2}\right) \ldots P\left(n_{k}\right)=Q\left(n_{1}\right) Q\left(n_{2}\right) \ldots Q\left(n_{k}\right)$, but $P(x) \neq Q(x)$

Thus, the children could have found the polynomial $Q(x)$ instead of $P(x)$, meaning the teacher did not achieve the required goal.

Example. Let $k=2017$. Set $n_{i}=4 i$ for $i=1,2, \ldots k$; suppose the teacher informs the children that

$P\left(n_{1}\right) P\left(n_{2}\right) \ldots P\left(n_{k}\right)=1$. Then the polynomial

$P(x)=\left(x-n_{1}\right)\left(x-n_{2}\right) \ldots\left(x-n_{k}\right)+1$ fits the condition.

Assume that some polynomial $Q(x)$ also fits the condition. Then, since $Q\left(n_{1}\right) Q\left(n_{2}\right) \ldots Q\left(n_{k}\right)=1$ and the coefficients of the polynomial $Q(x)$ are integers, $Q\left(n_{i}\right)= \pm 1$ for any $i=1,2, \ldots, k$.

If there exist such $i$ and $j$ that $Q\left(n_{i}\right)=1$, and $Q\left(n_{j}\right)=-1$, then the difference $Q\left(n_{i}\right)-Q\left(n_{j}\right)=2$ is not divisible by $n_{i}-n_{j}$, which contradicts the theorem of Bézout for integer polynomials (see problem $\underline{35562}$). Therefore, all values of $Q\left(n_{i}\right)$ are equal. However, all values cannot be equal to -1, since the product $Q\left(n_{1}\right) Q\left(n_{2}\right) \ldots Q\left(n_{k}\right)$ has an odd number of factors and the product would be -1. Thus, $Q\left(n_{i}\right)=1$ for any $i=1,2, \ldots, k$. Then the difference $P(x)-Q(x)$ is a polynomial of degree less than $k$, having $k$ distinct roots, meaning this polynomial is identically zero, and $P(x)=Q(x)$.

## Answer

For $k=2017$

question:
[ Ratio of areas of similar triangles ]

In a right triangle, the sine of the smaller angle is $\frac{1}{3}$. A line perpendicular to the hypotenuse divides the triangle into two equal areas. In what ratio does this line divide the hypotenuse?

meta.gold_solution:
Let $M$ be a point on the hypotenuse $AB$ of the right triangle $ABC$, $\sin \angle A = \frac{1}{3}$, and $N$ be a point on the leg $AC$ such that $MN \perp AB$ and $S_{\triangle AMN} = \frac{1}{2} S_{\triangle ABC}$.

Denote $BC = t$. Then,

$$
AB = \frac{BC}{\sin \angle A} = \frac{t}{\frac{1}{3}} = 3t.
$$

Triangle $ANM$ is similar to triangle $ABC$ with a similarity ratio equal to the square root of the ratio of the areas, i.e., $\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}$, so $MN = \frac{t}{\sqrt{2}}$.

From the right triangle $ANM$, we find that

$$
AN = \frac{MN}{\sin \angle A} = 3MN = \frac{3t}{\sqrt{2}}, \quad AM = \sqrt{AN^2 - MN^2} = \sqrt{\frac{9t^2}{2} - \frac{t^2}{2}} = 2t,
$$

thus $MB = AB - AM = 3t - 2t = t$. Therefore,

$$
\frac{AM}{MB} = \frac{2t}{t} = 2
$$

## Answer

$2: 1$

question:
15. Random Vectors. There are $n$ random vectors of the form $\left(y_{1}, y_{2}, y_{3}\right)$, where exactly one random coordinate is equal to 1, and the others are 0. They are added together. The result is a random vector $\vec{a}$ with coordinates $\left(Y_{1}, Y_{2}, Y_{3}\right)$.

a) (from 9th grade. 2 points). Find the expected value of the random variable $\vec{a}^{2}$.

b) (from 9th grade. 2 points). Prove that $|\vec{a}| \geq \frac{n}{\sqrt{3}}$.

meta.gold_solution:
Solution. a) Let's find the expected value $\mathrm{E} Y_{j}^{2}$. The quantity $Y_{j}$ is the number of ones among the numbers $y_{j}$, that is, this quantity is distributed according to the binomial law with probability $p=1 / 3$ and the number of trials $n$. Therefore,

$$
\mathrm{E} Y_{j}=n \cdot \frac{1}{3}=\frac{n}{3} \text { and } \mathrm{D} Y_{j}=n \cdot \frac{1}{3} \cdot \frac{2}{3}=\frac{2 n}{9}
$$

Then

$$
\mathrm{E}\left(\vec{a}^{2}\right)=\mathrm{E}\left(Y_{1}^{2}+Y_{2}^{2}+Y_{3}^{2}\right)=3 \mathrm{E} Y_{1}^{2}=3\left(\mathrm{D} Y_{1}+\mathrm{E}^{2} Y_{1}\right)=3 \cdot \frac{2 n}{9}+3 \cdot \frac{n^{2}}{9}=\frac{2 n+n^{2}}{3}
$$

b) We will use a known fact: the root mean square of non-negative numbers is not less than their arithmetic mean.

$$
\sqrt{Y_{1}^{2}+Y_{2}^{2}+Y_{3}^{2}}=\sqrt{\frac{Y_{1}^{2}+Y_{2}^{2}+Y_{3}^{2}}{3}} \cdot \sqrt{3} \geq \frac{Y_{1}+Y_{2}+Y_{3}}{3} \cdot \sqrt{3}=\frac{n}{\sqrt{3}}
$$

Answer: a) $\frac{2 n+n^{2}}{3}$.

question: 16. Check Digit (8th grade. 3 points). The Simple-Dairy Telephone Company “Simple-Telecom” uses three-digit telephone numbers. The equipment is old, so during connection, errors in individual digits of the transmitted subscriber number are possible - each digit, independently of the others, has a probability of $p=0.02$ of being replaced by some other random digit. To reduce the probability of incorrect connection, the company uses the following rule: the first digit of the number is always equal to the remainder of the sum of the two other digits divided by 10. For example, the numbers 000 and 156 are possible, while the number 234 is not. If the check digit is incorrect during connection, an error message is displayed. Find the probability that, despite the measures taken, an incorrect connection will occur.

meta.gold_solution:
Solution. Numbers that satisfy the rule will be called correct. The task is to ensure that, despite the erroneous digits, the number turns out to be correct.

If two digits are known, then the third digit is uniquely determined. Therefore, we will not consider the first digit separately, but will assume that all digits are equal.

An erroneous number cannot be correct if it differs from the correct one by only one digit. Differences in two or three digits are possible. To find the probability that an erroneous number will turn out to be correct, note that the probabilities of two or three erroneous digits are respectively

$$
C_{3}^{2} p^{2}(1-p) \text { and } C_{3}^{3} p^{3} .
$$

Let $r_{2}$ be the probability that the number turned out to be correct given that it has exactly two erroneous digits. Similarly, $r_{3}$ is the probability that a number with three erroneous digits turned out to be correct. Then the total probability that an erroneous number is correct is

$$
C_{3}^{2} p^{2}(1-p) r_{2}+C_{3}^{3} p^{3} r_{3}
$$

Suppose there are two erroneous digits. No matter what the first one is, the second is uniquely determined: the event "the erroneous number is correct" is favorable only for one value of the second digit out of nine possible erroneous ones. Therefore, if two erroneous digits are fixed, the number will be correct with a probability of $r_{2}=\frac{1}{9}$.

Let's explain this with an example. Suppose in the number 376 errors occurred, for definiteness, in the 2nd and 3rd digits. Suppose the 2nd digit became the digit 5 by mistake. Then we get the number $35 \mathrm{~A}$, where A can take one of 9 values (all except 6) with equal chances. But the number will be correct only if $\mathrm{A}=8$, since only in this case will the sum of the last two digits end in the digit 3.

Suppose there are three erroneous digits. No matter what the first erroneous digit is, the event "the number will be correct" is favorable for 8 values of the second digit out of 9 equally possible erroneous values, and for the third digit - only 1 out of 9. Therefore, $r_{3}=\frac{8}{9} \cdot \frac{1}{9}$.

Let's explain this again with an example. Suppose in the number 376 the first digit became the digit 2 by mistake. Then we get the number $2 \mathrm{AB}$. The digit A is erroneous, so A can take any of 9 values (all digits except 7) with equal chances. But if A takes the value 6, the number will be correct only if $\mathrm{B}=6$, but this is impossible because $\mathrm{B}$ is also an erroneous digit and cannot equal 6. Therefore, the event "the number is correct" is favorable for 8 values of A out of 9 possible erroneous ones and only one value of B out of 9 possible. The probability of this is $\frac{8}{9} \cdot \frac{1}{9}$. Therefore,

$$
C_{3}^{2} p^{2}(1-p) r_{2}+C_{3}^{3} p^{3} r_{3}=3 \cdot 0.02^{2} \cdot 0.98 \cdot \frac{1}{9}+1 \cdot 0.02^{3} \cdot \frac{8}{81} \approx 0.000131
$$

Answer: approximately $0.000131$.

question: A convex pentagon $ ABCDE$ is inscribed in a circle. The distances of $ A$ from the lines $ BC,CD,DE$ are $ a,b,c,$ respectively. Compute the distance of $ A$ from the line $ BE$.

meta.gold_solution:
To solve the problem, we will use the lemma provided and apply it to the given pentagon \(ABCDE\) inscribed in a circle. The lemma states that for a cyclic quadrilateral \(ABCD\) with a point \(P\) on its circumcircle, the product of the distances from \(P\) to opposite sides is equal. We will extend this idea to the pentagon \(ABCDE\).

1. **Identify the relevant distances and angles:**
   - Let \(A\) be the point from which we measure the distances to the lines \(BC\), \(CD\), and \(DE\), denoted as \(a\), \(b\), and \(c\) respectively.
   - We need to find the distance from \(A\) to the line \(BE\).

2. **Apply the lemma to the cyclic quadrilateral \(ABCD\):**
   - Consider the quadrilateral \(ABCD\) with \(A\) on its circumcircle.
   - Let \(X\), \(Y\), \(Z\), and \(V\) be the orthogonal projections of \(A\) on the sides \(AD\), \(AB\), \(BC\), and \(CD\) respectively.
   - According to the lemma, \(AX \cdot AZ = AY \cdot AV\).

3. **Relate the distances using the lemma:**
   - Since \(A\) is on the circumcircle, the angles \(\angle PAB\) and \(\angle PCD\) are equal.
   - Similarly, \(\angle PAX\) and \(\angle PCD\) are equal.
   - Therefore, \(AX \cdot AZ = AY \cdot AV\).

4. **Extend the lemma to the pentagon \(ABCDE\):**
   - Now consider the pentagon \(ABCDE\) with \(A\) on its circumcircle.
   - We need to find the distance from \(A\) to the line \(BE\).
   - Let \(d\) be the distance from \(A\) to the line \(BE\).

5. **Use the distances \(a\), \(b\), and \(c\) to find \(d\):**
   - By the lemma, the product of the distances from \(A\) to opposite sides of the cyclic quadrilateral is equal.
   - Therefore, \(a \cdot c = b \cdot d\).

6. **Solve for \(d\):**
   \[
   d = \frac{a \cdot c}{b}
   \]

The final answer is \(\boxed{\frac{a \cdot c}{b}}\).

question:
Find all functions $f: \mathbb{R} \rightarrow \mathbb{R}$ satisfying, for a given real $k$,

$$
\forall x, y \in \mathbb{R}, \quad f(2 x-2 y)+x=f(3 x)-f(2 y)+k y
$$

## Solutions of exercises

meta.gold_solution:
One of the main ideas in a functional equation with multiple terms is to make what is inside the parentheses equal, through a clever substitution, to obtain simplifications. For example, here, three substitutions are possible: $2 x - 2 y = 3 x$, $2 x - 2 y = 2 y$, or $3 x = 2 y$. We will only present the first one here, but it is worth noting that the third one also leads to a quick solution (try it!)

We want to have $2 x - 2 y = 3 x$. This is the case if we set $x = -2 y$. Let's see where this leads us:

$$
f(-6 y) - 2 y = f(-6 y) - f(2 y) + k y \Longleftrightarrow f(2 y) = (k + 2) y
$$

By setting $z = 2 y$, we get $f(z) = \frac{1}{2}(k + 2) z$

Let's test this solution:

$$
\begin{gathered}
\frac{1}{2}(k + 2)(2 x - 2 y) + x = \frac{1}{2}(k + 2) \times 3 x - \frac{1}{2}(k + 2) \times 2 y + k y \\
\Longleftrightarrow (2 k + 6) x - (2 k + 4) y = (3 k + 6) x - (k + 4) y \\
\quad \Longleftrightarrow (2 k + 6 = 3 k + 6 \text{ and } 2 k + 4 = k + 4) \Longleftrightarrow k = 0
\end{gathered}
$$

Therefore, there are solutions only for $k = 0$, in which case $\frac{1}{2}(k + 2) x = x$, and the function $f(x) = x$ is indeed a solution.

## Injectivity, Surjectivity, and Bijectivity

We now introduce the essential concepts of injective, surjective, and bijective functions. These are properties that we can try to deduce from the statement to get clues about the solutions.

## Definition 2.

A function is said to be injective if the images of two distinct elements by $f$ are distinct. In other words, if $a$ and $b$ belong to the domain of definition of $f$ and $a \neq b$, then $f(a) \neq f(b)$. Thus, every element in the codomain has a unique preimage.

## Definition 3.

A function is said to be surjective if every element in the codomain has at least one preimage. In other words, if $f: A \rightarrow B$, then for every $y \in B$ there exists an $x \in A$ such that $f(x) = y$.

## Definition 4.

A function is said to be bijective if it is both injective and surjective.

## Remark 5.

A function is therefore bijective if every element in the codomain has a unique preimage.

## Remark 6.

To show that a function is injective, we often use the contrapositive: we show that if two elements $a$ and $b$ satisfy $f(a) = f(b)$, then $a = b$.

## Remark 7.

To show that a function is surjective, we generally try to reduce it to an equation of the form $f(A) = B$, where $A$ and $B$ are expressions that depend on a variable $x$. If $B$ covers the entire codomain of $f$ as $x$ covers the same set, then $f$ is surjective.

question:
1. Find all positive integers $n$ which are not powers of 2 and which satisfy the equation $n=3 D+5 d$, where $D$ (and d) denote the greatest (and the least) numbers among the all odd divisors of $n$ which are larger than 1.

(Tomáš Jurík)

meta.gold_solution:
Solution. Let $n=p_{1}^{\alpha_{1}} p_{2}^{\alpha_{2}} \ldots p_{k}^{\alpha_{k}}$ be the prime factorization of a satisfactory number $n$. Here $p_{1}2$. Consequently, there are infinitely many solutions in the case (ii) and all of them are given by $n=2^{3} p_{2}^{1}=8 p_{2}$, where $p_{2}$ is any odd prime number.

Answer. All the solutions $n$ are: $n=60, n=100$ and $n=8 p$, where $p$ is any odd prime number.

Remark. Let us show that the above solution can be presented more simply, if the "full" prime factorization of $n$ is replaced by a "partial" factorization $n=2^{\alpha} p l$, in which $2^{\alpha}$ is the greatest power of 2 dividing $n, p$ is the smallest prime divisor of $n$ and and $l$ is and odd number which has no prime divisor smaller than $p$ (thus we
have either $l=1$, or $l \geqslant p$ ). Using this factorization, we can write $D=p l, d=p$ and hence our task is to solve the equation

$$
n=2^{\alpha} p l=3 p l+5 p \quad \text { or } \quad\left(2^{\alpha}-3\right) l=5 \text {. }
$$

It follows that either $l=1$ and $2^{\alpha}-3=5$, or $l=5$ and $2^{\alpha}-3=1$. In the first case we have $\alpha=3$ and thus $n=8 p$, where $p$ is any prime number. In the second case it holds that $l=5, \alpha=2$ and thus $n=20 p$, but $5=l \geqslant p$ implies that $p \in\{3,5\}$, so there are only two solutions $n \in\{60,100\}$.

Another solution. The given equation $n=3 D+5 d$ implies that $n>3 D$ and $n \leqslant 3 D+5 D=8 D$ (because of $d \leqslant D$ ). Since the ratio $n: D$ must be a power of 2 , it follows from $3<n: D \leqslant 8$ that either (i) $n=4 D$, or (ii) $n=8 D$.

(i) The case $n=4 D$. From $4 D=n=3 D+5 d$ we have $D=5 d$ and thus $n=4 D=20 d$. Since $d$ must be a prime odd divisor of $n$ which is a multiple of 5 , we conclude that $p \in\{3,5\}$ and hence $n \in\{60,100\}$ (both the values are clearly satisfactory).

(ii) $n=8 D$. Our way of deriving the inequality $n \leqslant 8 D$ implies now that $D=d$ a hence $D$ is an (odd) prime number. All such $n=8 D$ are solutions indeed.

x_{1}^{4}+x_{2}^{4} & =\left(x_{1}^{2}+x_{2}^{2}\right)^{2}-2 x_{1}^{2} x_{2}^{2} \\

$$

question: In each cell of a table $8\times 8$ lives a knight or a liar. By the tradition, the knights always say the truth and the liars always lie. All the inhabitants of the table say the following statement "The number of liars in my column is (strictly) greater than the number of liars in my row". Determine how many possible configurations are compatible with the statement.

meta.gold_solution:
1. **Understanding the Problem:**
   - We have an $8 \times 8$ table.
   - Each cell contains either a knight (who always tells the truth) or a liar (who always lies).
   - Each inhabitant states: "The number of liars in my column is strictly greater than the number of liars in my row."

2. **Analyzing the Statement:**
   - For a knight, the statement must be true.
   - For a liar, the statement must be false.

3. **Considering the Implications:**
   - If a knight is in a cell, then the number of liars in the column must be greater than the number of liars in the row.
   - If a liar is in a cell, then the number of liars in the column must not be greater than the number of liars in the row.

4. **Exploring the Configuration:**
   - Let’s denote the number of liars in row $i$ as $r_i$ and in column $j$ as $c_j$.
   - For a knight in cell $(i, j)$, the condition $c_j > r_i$ must hold.
   - For a liar in cell $(i, j)$, the condition $c_j \leq r_i$ must hold.

5. **Considering the Columns and Rows:**
   - Suppose there are two columns $c_1$ and $c_2$.
   - If $c_1$ has more liars than $c_2$, then there must be a liar in $c_1$ and a knight in $c_2$ in some row $r$.
   - This leads to a contradiction because if $c_1 \geq c_2$, then $c_1 \leq r < c_2$ cannot hold.

6. **Conclusion on Columns:**
   - Therefore, all columns must have the same number of liars.

7. **Considering the Rows:**
   - If we have a liar, the proposition is always satisfied because $r_i = n \geq c_j$.
   - If we have a knight, the proposition is almost always satisfied because $r_i = 0 < c_j$ if there is at least one liar in the row.

8. **Counting the Configurations:**
   - We can choose freely any row, with the exception of all knights.
   - This leads to $2^8 - 1 = 255$ possibilities.

The final answer is $\boxed{255}$.

[Solution] We first prove that $S$ has at most 5 elements.
In fact, if $S$ has at least 6 elements, then the number of non-empty subsets of $S$ with at most 4 elements is at least
$$
C_{6}^{1}+C_{6}^{2}+C_{6}^{3}+C_{6}^{4}=56 \text { (subsets) }
$$

The sum of these subsets does not exceed 54 (i.e., $15+14+13+12=54$). By the pigeonhole principle, among the 56 positive integers not exceeding 54, at least two numbers are equal, i.e., at least two subsets have the same sum. If these two subsets are disjoint, it contradicts the condition that “the sums of any two disjoint subsets of $S$ are not equal.” If these two subsets intersect, removing the common elements will still lead to a contradiction.
Therefore, $S$ has at most 5 elements.
Next, we construct this 5-element set to make its elements as large as possible (thus making the sum of the set as large as possible).
After $S$ contains $15, 14, 13$, it cannot contain 12, otherwise $15+12=14+13$;
$S$ can contain 11, but it cannot contain 10 and 9, otherwise $15+10=14+11, 15+$ $9=13+11$;
The last element is taken as 8, then
$$
\begin{array}{l}
S=\{15,14,13,11,8\} \\
15+14+13+11+8=61
\end{array}
$$

Thus, the largest possible sum is 61.

question: Let's determine the largest of the $A$ numbers for which the following statement holds. No matter how we write down the first 100 positive integers, there will always be ten consecutive numbers in the sequence whose sum is at least $A$.

meta.gold_solution:
Let the first 100 positive integers be in some order $a_{1}, a_{2}, \ldots, a_{100}$. Their sum is

$$
a_{1}+a_{2}+\ldots+a_{100}=(1+100)+(2+99)+\ldots+(50+51)=50 \cdot 101=5050
$$

Therefore, if we divide the terms of the sum $a_{1}+a_{2}+\ldots+a_{100}$ into ten groups of ten, there will be a group where the sum of the numbers is at least $5050: 10=505$.

This means that no matter how we write the first 100 positive integers, there will always be ten consecutive numbers in the sequence whose sum is at least 505. The sought number is therefore at least 505.

If there is an order of the first 100 positive integers where the sum of any ten consecutive numbers is at most 505, then we are done; in this case, the sought number is exactly 505, because choosing a larger number $A$ would not satisfy the condition for the given order. The following order is exactly such:

$$
100,1,99,2, \ldots, 51,50
$$

Here, the numbers in the odd positions decrease from 100 to 51, and the numbers in the even positions increase from 1 to 50. The sum of any two consecutive numbers is either 101 or 100, so the sum of any ten consecutive numbers is 505 or 500, depending on whether the first of the ten numbers is in an odd or even position in the sequence.

The sought number is therefore 505.

question:
Tokaeva I.

Let $F_{1}, F_{2}, F_{3}, \ldots$ be a sequence of convex quadrilaterals, where $F_{k+1}$ (for $k=1,2,3, \ldots$) is obtained by cutting $F_{k}$ along a diagonal, flipping one of the parts, and gluing it back along the cut line to the other part. What is the maximum number of different quadrilaterals that this sequence can contain? (Different polygons are those that cannot be made to coincide by a movement.)

meta.gold_solution:
Let $ABCD$ be the original quadrilateral $F_{1}$. We can assume that each time the half of the quadrilateral containing side $CD$ is flipped, while side $AB$ remains stationary. In this process, the sum of angle $A$ and the opposite angle does not change. Additionally, the set of side lengths does not change. However, the three lengths (sides other than $AB$) can be ordered in only six ways.

We will prove that if two resulting quadrilaterals $ABKL$ and $ABMN$ have the same ordered side lengths ($BK = BM$, $KL = MN$, $LA = NA$), then the quadrilaterals are equal. It is sufficient to prove the equality of the diagonals $AK$ and $AM$. Assuming, for example, that $AK > AM$, we get $\angle ABK > \angle ABM$, $\angle ALK > \angle ANM$, which contradicts the equality of the sums $\angle ABK + \angle ALK$ and $\angle ABM + \angle ANM$.

Six different quadrilaterals will result from any quadrilateral where all sides are different, the sums of opposite angles are also different, and the quadrilateral remains convex and does not degenerate into a triangle during transformations. Only quadrilaterals with the reverse order of sides might be suspected of being equal, but they are not equal either, since flipping one of them will not align the sums of opposite angles. The highlighted condition is satisfied, for example, for quadrilaterals whose area is greater than half the product of the two longest sides: this inequality is clearly not true for non-convex and degenerate quadrilaterals. A specific example: a right trapezoid with bases 3 and 6 and height 4.

## Answer

6 quadrilaterals.

question:
Josefina the Quail dances by the marsh, using steps of double length — short steps measure $45 \mathrm{~cm}$, long steps $60 \mathrm{~cm}$. Over time, she has worn an oval path, which she dances around repeatedly during long nights. If she repeats three long steps forward and one short step back, then the ninetieth step will bring her exactly back to where she started. If she repeats three short steps forward and one long step back, she also ends up exactly where she started.

Which step will bring Josefina back to the original spot in the second case?

(M. Petrová)

meta.gold_solution:
With one large four-step (three long steps forward and one short step back), Josefa moves $135 \, \text{cm} (3 \cdot 60 - 45 = 135)$. Ninety steps consist of 22 large four-steps and two long steps $(90 = 22 \cdot 4 + 2)$. Therefore, Josefa's circuit measures $3090 \, \text{cm} (22 \cdot 135 + 2 \cdot 60 = 3090)$.

With one small four-step (three short steps forward and one long step back), Josefa moves $75 \, \text{cm} (3 \cdot 45 - 60 = 75)$. Forty such four-steps—i.e., 160 steps—move her $3000 \, \text{cm} (40 \cdot 75 = 3000)$, ensuring she does not exceed her original position (before the last backward step, she is at a distance of $3060 \, \text{cm}$). The remaining $90 \, \text{cm}$ she covers in the next two steps $(2 \cdot 45 = 90)$.

Josefa will dance back to her original position on the 162nd step.

Note. To illustrate the situation, we provide some distances (in $\text{cm}$) corresponding to the dance steps used in the second case:

| step | 1 | 2 | 3 | 4 | 5 | 6 | $\ldots$ |
| :---: | :---: | :---: | :---: | :---: | :---: | :---: | :---: |
| distance | 45 | 90 | 135 | 75 | 120 | 165 | $\ldots$ |

| step | $\ldots$ | 158 | 159 | 160 | 161 | 162 | 163 |
| :---: | :---: | :---: | :---: | :---: | :---: | :---: | :---: |
| distance | $\ldots$ | 3015 | 3060 | 3000 | 3045 | 3090 | 3135 |

From this, it is also clear that different steps correspond to different distances.

Evaluation. 2 points for the length of Josefa's circuit; 2 points for the number of steps in the second case; 2 points for clarity and quality of the commentary.

question: Let's construct the projections of a cylinder, which is tangent to two given planes and the first trace (circle) of the projection axis. (How many solutions are possible?)

meta.gold_solution:
1. Solution. Let's construct the base circle of the cylinder, that is, draw a tangent circle between the axis and the two first traces. Once the base circle of the cylinder is established, we need to find the direction of its generators. However, the generators are parallel to lines that are parallel to both planes.

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2024_05_02_ab314ebff96f57813f41g-1.jpg?height=524&width=637&top_left_y=318&top_left_x=728)

One such line is the intersection of the two planes. Therefore, let's find the first and second projections of the intersection line, which will give us the direction of the first and second projections of the generators.

The problem has four possible solutions. This is natural because four tangent circles can be drawn to three intersecting lines. In this case, the three lines are the axis and the first traces.

(Tóbiás J. László.)

2. Solution. The first projection of the base circle should be inscribed in the triangle formed by the given traces and the projection axis. Therefore, four solutions are possible. The direction of the cylinder is determined by the intersection line of the planes, as this is the only line for which we can find parallels in both planes.

(Lázár Lajos, Budapest.)

question: Problem 9.4. At a round table, 40 knights and 10 samurais are sitting. Exactly 7 knights have a samurai as their right neighbor. What is the maximum number of knights that could be sitting next to two knights?

meta.gold_solution:
# Answer: 32.

Solution. Let's divide the people sitting at the table into alternating groups of consecutive knights and consecutive samurais. From the condition, it follows that there are exactly 14 such groups (7 groups of knights and 7 groups of samurais), since the 7 knights mentioned in the condition are precisely the rightmost knights in the groups of knights.

Note that at least 8 knights do not sit next to two knights: these are the 7 knights mentioned in the condition and at least 1 leftmost knight in a group of more than one knight (such a group exists because there are 7 groups and 40 knights). Therefore, no more than $40-8=32$ knights sit between two knights.

Now let's provide an example. For this, we will take 6 groups of knights consisting of 1 person each and one group of 34, while the samurais can be distributed arbitrarily among 7 groups (not forgetting that the groups of knights and samurais alternate). It is clear that 32 non-edge knights from the "large" group of knights are the ones we are looking for.

question: 1. To each vertex of a regular 66-gon, we assign one of the numbers 1 or -1. For each segment connecting two of its vertices (a side or a diagonal), we then write down the product of the numbers $v$ at its endpoints and sum all the numbers for the individual segments. Determine the smallest possible and the smallest non-negative value of such a sum.

meta.gold_solution:
SOLUTION. Assume that some $k$ vertices $(0 \leqq k \leqq 66)$ of a regular 66-gon are assigned the number 1, and the remaining $66-k$ vertices are assigned the number -1. According to the conditions of the problem, we assign the number 1 to each segment connecting two vertices with the number 1. There are a total of $\frac{1}{2} k(k-1)$ such segments. Similarly, we assign the number 1 to each segment whose both endpoints are assigned the number -1. There are a total of $\frac{1}{2}(66-k)(65-k)$ such segments. Finally, we assign the number -1 to each of the remaining segments (and there are $k(66-k)$ of them).

The value $S$ of the sum of all numbers assigned to individual segments (sides or diagonals of the considered 66-gon) is therefore

$$
\begin{aligned}
S & =\frac{k(k-1)}{2}+\frac{(66-k)(65-k)}{2}-k(66-k)= \\
& =2 k^{2}-2 \cdot 66 k+65 \cdot 33= \\
& =2(k-33)^{2}-33 .
\end{aligned}
$$

We see that $S \geqq-33$ always holds, and equality apparently occurs for $k=33$.

Now we will determine for which $k(0 \leqq k \leqq 66)$ the inequality $S \geqq 0$ is satisfied. These will be the $k$ for which $|k-33| \geqq \sqrt{33 / 2}>4$, so for non-negative values of $S$, it will certainly hold that $S \geqq 2 \cdot 5^{2}-33=17$. Equality occurs when $|k-33|=5$ or $k \in\{28,38\}$.

Conclusion. The examined expression attains its smallest value $S=-33$ for $k=33$. The smallest possible non-negative value of the examined sum is then $S=17$ for $k=28$ or $k=38$.

N2. Determine the smallest value of the expression $V=3 x^{2}+4 x+5$, where $x$ is any real number, and also find its smallest integer value. [The smallest possible value of the expression $V$ is $\frac{11}{3}$, which is achieved for $x=-\frac{2}{3}$. The smallest integer value of the examined expression is $V=4$ and is achieved for $x=-1$ or $x=-\frac{1}{3}$.]

N3. Assign one of the numbers 1 or -1 to each vertex of a regular 63-gon. To each of its sides, we assign the product of the numbers at its vertices and sum all the numbers for the individual sides. Find the smallest possible non-negative value of such a sum. [63-B-I-1]

question:
Example 3 If the function $f: \mathbf{R} \rightarrow \mathbf{R}$ satisfies for all real numbers $x$,
$$
\sqrt{2 f(x)}-\sqrt{2 f(x)-f(2 x)} \geqslant 2
$$

then the function $f$ is said to have property $P$. Find the largest real number $\lambda$ such that if the function $f$ has property $P$, then for all real numbers $x$, $f(x) \geqslant \lambda$ always holds.

meta.gold_solution:
Solve: From equation (1) we get
$$
\begin{array}{l}
f(x) \geqslant 2, \\
\sqrt{2 f(x)}-2 \geqslant \sqrt{2 f(x)-f(2 x)} .
\end{array}
$$

Squaring both sides of equation (2) we get
$$
\begin{array}{l}
f(2 x) \geqslant 4 \sqrt{2 f(x)}-4 \\
\Rightarrow f(x) \geqslant 4, \text { and } f(x) \geqslant 4 \sqrt{2 f\left(\frac{x}{2}\right)}-4 .
\end{array}
$$

Conjecture:
$f(x)=c$ has property $P \Leftrightarrow \sqrt{2 c}-\sqrt{c} \geqslant 2$
$$
\Leftrightarrow c \geqslant 12+8 \sqrt{2} \text {. }
$$

It is easy to verify that $f(x)=12+8 \sqrt{2}$ has property $P$, thus $12+8 \sqrt{2} \geqslant \lambda$.
Next, we prove: If function $f(x)$ has property $P$, then for all real numbers $x$,
$$
f(x) \geqslant 12+8 \sqrt{2} \text {. }
$$

Define the sequence $\left\{a_{n}\right\}: a_{0}=2, a_{n+1}=4 \sqrt{2 a_{n}}-4$.
We can prove: (1) $a_{n}<a_{n+1}$.
In fact,
$$
\begin{array}{l}
a_{n+1}-a_{n}=4 \sqrt{2 a_{n}}-4 \sqrt{2 a_{n-1}} \\
=4 \sqrt{2}\left(\sqrt{a_{n}}-\sqrt{a_{n-1}}\right) .
\end{array}
$$

By mathematical induction, it is easy to get $a_{n}<a_{n+1}$.
(2) $a_{n}<12+8 \sqrt{2}$.

When $n=0$, $a_{0}=2<12+8 \sqrt{2}$.
Assume when $n=k$, $a_{k}<12+8 \sqrt{2}$.
Then $a_{k+1}=4 \sqrt{2 a_{k}}-4$
$$
<4 \sqrt{24+16 \sqrt{2}}-4=12+8 \sqrt{2} \text {. }
$$

In summary, the sequence $\left\{a_{n}\right\}$ is monotonically increasing and bounded above. Therefore, it has a limit.
Let $\lim _{n \rightarrow+\infty} a_{n}=a$.
Then $a=4 \sqrt{2 a}-4 \Rightarrow a=12+8 \sqrt{2}$.
(3) For any non-negative integer $n$ and any real number $x$, $f(x) \geqslant a_{n}$.
When $n=0$, $f(x) \geqslant 2=a_{0}$.
Assume the proposition holds for $n$, i.e., for any real number $x$, $f(x) \geqslant a_{n}$.
Thus $f(x) \geqslant 4 \sqrt{2 f\left(\frac{x}{2}\right)}-4$
$\geqslant 4 \sqrt{2 a_{n}}-4=a_{n+1}$.
Let $n \rightarrow+\infty$.
Then $f(x) \geqslant \lim _{n \rightarrow+\infty} a_{n+1}=a=12+8 \sqrt{2}$.
In summary, $\lambda_{\max }=12+8 \sqrt{2}$.

question:

$$u_{n+1} u_{n-1}=k u_{n}$$

where $k$ is some fixed positive integer. If
$$u_{2000}=2000$$

find all possible values of $k$.

meta.gold_solution:
［Solution］ Let $u_{1}=u$. By the problem statement,
$$u_{2}=\frac{k u_{1}}{u_{0}}=k u$$

If $u=0$, then $u_{1}=0, u_{2}=0$. If $u_{t-1}=0$, then $k u_{t}=u_{t-1} \cdot$ $u_{t+1}=0$, hence $u_{t}=0$. Therefore, for any positive integer $n, u_{n}=0$. This contradicts $u_{2000}=2000$. Thus, $u \neq 0$.

By the problem statement, after calculation we get
$$\begin{array}{ll}
u_{3}=\frac{k u_{2}}{u_{1}}=k^{2}, & u_{4}=\frac{k u_{3}}{u_{2}}=\frac{k^{2}}{u}, \\
u_{5}=\frac{k u_{4}}{u_{3}}=\frac{k}{u}, & u_{6}=\frac{k u_{5}}{u_{4}}=1, \\
u_{7}=\frac{k u_{6}}{u_{5}}=u . &
\end{array}$$

From this, we can see that the given sequence is a periodic sequence with a period of 6. Therefore, by
$$2000=6 \times 333+2$$

we have
$$u_{2000}=u_{2}=k u,$$

Thus, $k$ should satisfy
$$\left\{\begin{array}{l}
k u=2000, \\
\frac{k}{u} \text { is an integer, }
\end{array}\right.$$

question: What is the maximal dimension of a linear subspace $ V$ of the vector space of real $ n \times n$ matrices such that for all $ A$ in $ B$ in $ V$, we have $ \text{trace}\left(AB\right) \equal{} 0$ ?

meta.gold_solution:
1. **Define the Problem in Terms of Bilinear Forms:**
   We start by noting that the trace function $\text{trace}(AB)$ defines a symmetric bilinear form on the space of $n \times n$ real matrices, denoted as $Mat_n(\mathbb{R})$. Specifically, for matrices $A, B \in Mat_n(\mathbb{R})$, we define the bilinear form $(A, B) := \text{trace}(AB)$.

2. **Properties of the Bilinear Form:**
   The bilinear form $(A, B) := \text{trace}(AB)$ is symmetric because $\text{trace}(AB) = \text{trace}(BA)$ for any matrices $A$ and $B$. This symmetry implies that the form is well-suited for analysis using tools from the theory of quadratic forms and orthogonal spaces.

3. **Decomposition Using Witt's Theorem:**
   According to Witt's theorem, any symmetric bilinear form on a vector space over a field can be decomposed into a direct sum of orthogonal subspaces. For the space $Mat_n(\mathbb{R})$, this decomposition is:
   \[
   Mat_n(\mathbb{R}) = L_0 \oplus L_{an} \oplus L_h
   \]
   where:
   - $L_0$ is the kernel of the bilinear form (matrices $A$ such that $\text{trace}(AB) = 0$ for all $B$),
   - $L_{an}$ is the anisotropic part (contains no isotropic vectors),
   - $L_h$ is the hyperbolic part (contains pairs of isotropic vectors).

4. **Analyzing the Kernel $L_0$:**
   We claim that $L_0 = 0$. To see why, consider any non-zero matrix $A$. We can always find a matrix $B$ such that $\text{trace}(AB) \neq 0$. For example, if $A$ has a non-zero entry $a_{ij}$, we can choose $B$ to be a matrix with a $1$ in the $(j,i)$ position and zeros elsewhere. This choice ensures that $\text{trace}(AB) = a_{ij} \neq 0$. Hence, $L_0 = 0$.

5. **Dimension of $L_{an}$:**
   The anisotropic part $L_{an}$ contains all diagonal matrices because no diagonal matrix can be isotropic (i.e., $\text{trace}(A^2) \neq 0$ for any non-zero diagonal matrix $A$). The dimension of the space of diagonal matrices is $n$, so $\dim L_{an} \geq n$.

6. **Dimension of $L_h$:**
   Since $L_0 = 0$, the remaining part of the space is $L_{an} \oplus L_h$. The total dimension of $Mat_n(\mathbb{R})$ is $n^2$, so:
   \[
   \dim L_{an} + \dim L_h = n^2
   \]
   Given that $\dim L_{an} \geq n$, it follows that:
   \[
   \dim L_h \leq n^2 - n = n(n-1)
   \]

7. **Maximal Isotropic Subspace:**
   We seek the dimension of a maximal isotropic subspace $V$ within $Mat_n(\mathbb{R})$. A maximal isotropic subspace in $L_h$ (since $L_{an}$ contains no isotropic vectors) must have a hyperbolic counterpart. By a well-known lemma in the theory of quadratic forms, the dimension of any maximal isotropic subspace $V$ satisfies:
   \[
   2 \dim V \leq \dim L_h \leq n(n-1)
   \]
   Therefore:
   \[
   \dim V \leq \frac{n(n-1)}{2}
   \]

8. **Example to Achieve the Bound:**
   The space of upper triangular matrices (excluding the diagonal) provides an example of a subspace where $\text{trace}(AB) = 0$ for all $A, B$ in the subspace. The dimension of this subspace is indeed $\frac{n(n-1)}{2}$, showing that the bound is achievable.

Conclusion:
\[
\boxed{\frac{n(n-1)}{2}}
\]

question:
Problem 6.3. In a new math textbook, there are a total of 91 problems. Yura started solving them in the mornings, beginning on September 6.

Every morning, starting from September 7, he solves one fewer problem than the previous morning (until the problems run out).

By the evening of September 8, Yura realized that there were still 46 problems left to solve in the textbook. On which day of September will he finish solving the textbook?

meta.gold_solution:
Answer: 12.

Solution. In the first 3 days, Yura solved $91-46=45$ problems. Let's say on September 7th, he solved $z$ problems, then on September 6th, he solved $(z+1)$ problems, and on September 8th, he solved $(z-1)$ problems. We get that $45=(z+1)+z+(z-1)=3 z$, from which $z=15$.

Since $91=16+15+14+13+12+11+10$, Yura will solve problems for exactly 7 days, from September 6th to September 12th.

question:
For which natural numbers $n$ is the value of the following expression a perfect square?

$$
n^{5}-n^{4}-2 n^{3}+2 n^{2}+n-1
$$

meta.gold_solution:
For $n=1$, the value of the given expression is 0, so $(n-1)$ can be factored out:

$$
(n-1)\left(n^{4}-2 n^{2}+1\right)
$$

The second factor of the product is a perfect square $\left(n^{2}-1\right)^{2}$, and if $n$ is a natural number, this is the square of a natural number. Thus, the product is a perfect square precisely when either the first factor is a perfect square, or the second factor is 0.

In the latter case, $|n|=1$, and thus for natural numbers, $n=1$. In the former case, $n=k^{2}+1$, where $k$ is an integer. Since choosing $k=0$ gives us the case $n=1$, the given expression is a perfect square if and only if $n=k^{2}+1$, where $k$ is an integer.

Next, we prove: When 18 numbers are taken, there exist two numbers whose ratio lies within the interval $\left[\frac{2}{3}, \frac{3}{2}\right]$.

question: Anna and Zsófi take turns rolling a die, and they always add the rolled number to the sum of the numbers rolled so far. The one who, after their roll, makes the sum first divisible by 4 wins. If Anna starts, what is the probability that she wins?

meta.gold_solution:
Solution. Regardless of the sum of the numbers rolled up to a given moment - unless it is divisible by 4, in which case the game ends - the next player can roll a number that ensures a win: if the sum is of the form $4k+1$, they can roll a 3; if it is of the form $4k+2$, they can roll a 2 or a 6; and if it is of the form $4k+3$, they can roll a 1 or a 5.

Thus, with each roll, there is at least a $\frac{1}{6}$ chance that the game will end with the next roll. The probability that the game has not ended after $n$ rolls is at most $\left(\frac{5}{6}\right)^{n}$, and this value approaches zero. Therefore, the game ends with probability 1.

Suppose that at a given state of the game, the sum of the rolled numbers is of the form $4k+r$ $(0 \leq r \leq 3)$. If $P_{r}$ denotes the probability that the next player - who could be either Anna or Zsófi, let's call them $X$ - eventually wins, then this probability clearly depends only on the remainder $r$. On the other hand, since the game ends, the other player, who follows $X$, wins with probability $1-P_{r}$. Here, it is clear that $P_{0}=0$, since $X$ has already lost. If $X$'s roll results in a sum of the form $4k+r'$, then now it is not $X$ who follows, so according to the above, $1-P_{r'}$ is the probability that $X$ wins. In the following, we use this simple observation when writing down the probabilities $P_{r}$.

Let's examine the non-zero remainders; let $r=1$ first, and see what the probability is that $X$ wins the game in the situation that arises after their possible rolls. If they roll a 3 - the probability of which is $\frac{1}{6}$ - then they win with probability $\left(1-P_{0}\right)=1$. If they roll a 1 or a 5 - the probability of which is $\frac{1}{3}$ - then, arriving at a number of the form $4k+2$, they win with probability $\left(1-P_{2}\right)$. Similarly, if they roll a 2 or a 6 - the probability of which is also $\frac{1}{3}$ - then they win with probability $\left(1-P_{3}\right)$, and if they roll a 4, they win with probability $\left(1-P_{1}\right)$. Therefore:

$$
P_{1}=\frac{1}{6}\left(1-P_{0}\right)+\frac{1}{3}\left(1-P_{2}\right)+\frac{1}{3}\left(1-P_{3}\right)+\frac{1}{6}\left(1-P_{1}\right)
$$

Similarly, the probabilities $P_{2}$ and $P_{3}$ can be written as:

$$
\begin{aligned}
& P_{2}=\frac{1}{3}\left(1-P_{0}\right)+\frac{1}{3}\left(1-P_{3}\right)+\frac{1}{6}\left(1-P_{1}\right)+\frac{1}{6}\left(1-P_{2}\right), \quad \text { and } \\
& P_{3}=\frac{1}{3}\left(1-P_{0}\right)+\frac{1}{3}\left(1-P_{1}\right)+\frac{1}{6}\left(1-P_{2}\right)+\frac{1}{6}\left(1-P_{3}\right)
\end{aligned}
$$

Rearranging the three equations, we get the following system of equations:

$$
7 P_{1}+2 P_{2}+2 P_{3}=6
$$

From (2):

$P_{1}+7 P_{2}+2 P_{3}=6$

From (3):

$2 P_{1}+P_{2}+7 P_{3}=6$.

Solving the system of equations, we find that $P_{1}=\frac{50}{99}, P_{2}=\frac{60}{99}, P_{3}=\frac{62}{99}$.

Now let's turn to the game between the two players, Anna and Zsófi. If Anna rolls a number of the form $4k+r$ on her first turn, then according to the above, she wins with probability $1-P_{0}=1$ if $r=0$; and with probability $1-P_{r}$ if $r=1,2,3$. Since she rolls a 0 or 3 remainder with probability $\frac{1}{6}$ and a 1 (1 and 5) or 2 (2 and 6) with probability $\frac{1}{3}$, the probability that Anna wins as the starting player is:

$$
\frac{1}{6}\left(1-P_{0}\right)+\frac{1}{3}\left(1-P_{1}\right)+\frac{1}{3}\left(1-P_{2}\right)+\frac{1}{6}\left(1-P_{3}\right)=\frac{1}{6}+\frac{1}{3} \cdot \frac{49}{99}+\frac{1}{3} \cdot \frac{39}{99}+\frac{1}{6} \cdot \frac{37}{99}=\frac{52}{99}
$$

which is slightly greater than $\frac{1}{2}$.

Remark. Many omitted the proof that the game ends with probability 1, thus the above reasoning is incomplete.

question: 14. Solve the inequality $\log _{2}\left(x^{12}+3 x^{10}+5 x^{8}+3 x^{6}+1\right)<1+\log _{2}\left(x^{4}+1\right)$.

meta.gold_solution:
$$
\begin{array}{l}
\text { Solution 1: Original inequality } \Rightarrow x^{12}+3 x^{10}+5 x^{8}+3 x^{6}+1<2\left(x^{4}+1\right) \\
\Rightarrow x^{12}+3 x^{10}+5 x^{8}+3 x^{6}-2 x^{4}-1<0 \\
\Rightarrow\left(x^{4}+x^{2}-1\right)\left(x^{8}+2 x^{6}+4 x^{4}+x^{2}+1\right)<0 \\
\Rightarrow x^{4}+x^{2}-1<0 \Rightarrow 0 \leqslant x^{2}<\frac{\sqrt{5}-1}{2} \Rightarrow x \in\left(-\sqrt{\frac{\sqrt{5}-1}{2}}, \sqrt{\frac{\sqrt{5}-1}{2}}\right) .
\end{array}
$$

Solution 2: Original inequality $\Rightarrow x^{12}+3 x^{10}+5 x^{8}+3 x^{6}+1<2\left(x^{4}+1\right)$
$$
\begin{array}{l}
\Rightarrow x^{12}+3 x^{10}+3 x^{8}+x^{6}+2\left(x^{8}+x^{6}\right)<2 x^{4}+1 \\
\Rightarrow x^{6}+3 x^{4}+3 x^{2}+1+2\left(x^{2}+1\right)<\frac{2}{x^{2}}+\frac{1}{x^{6}} \\
\Rightarrow\left(x^{2}+1\right)^{3}+2\left(x^{2}+1\right)<\left(\frac{1}{x^{2}}\right)^{3}+\frac{2}{x^{2}} \Rightarrow x^{2}+1<\frac{1}{x^{2}} \\
\Rightarrow x^{4}+x^{2}-1<0 \Rightarrow 0 \leqslant x^{2}<\frac{\sqrt{5}-1}{2} \Rightarrow x \in\left(-\sqrt{\frac{\sqrt{5}-1}{2}}, \sqrt{\frac{\sqrt{5}-1}{2}}\right) .
\end{array}
$$

question:
Example 9 Given that $f(x)$ is a function defined on the set of natural numbers $\mathrm{N}$, satisfying $f(1)=\frac{3}{2}$, and for any $x, y \in \mathrm{N}$, there is $f(x+y)=\left(1+\frac{y}{x+1}\right) f(x)+\left(1+\frac{x}{y+1}\right) f(y)+x^{2} y+x y+x y^{2}$. Find $f(x)$.

Translate the above text into English, please retain the original text's line breaks and format, and output the translation result directly.

meta.gold_solution:
Solution: In the original functional equation, let $y=1$, and use $f(1)=\frac{3}{2}$, we get $f(x+1)=\left(1+\frac{1}{x+1}\right) f(x)+\left(1+\frac{x}{2}\right) \cdot \frac{3}{2}+x^{2}+2 x$.
Rearranging gives $\frac{f(x+1)}{x+2}-\frac{f(x)}{x+1}=x+\frac{3}{4}$.
Let $x=1,2, \cdots, n-1$ to get
$$
\begin{array}{l}
\frac{f(2)}{3}-\frac{f(1)}{2}=1+\frac{3}{4} \\
\frac{f(3)}{4}-\frac{f(2)}{3}=2+\frac{3}{4} \\
\cdots \cdots
\end{array}
$$
$$
\frac{f(n)}{n+1}-\frac{f(n-1)}{n}=(n-1)+\frac{3}{4}
$$

Adding the above equations, we get
$$
\frac{f(n)}{n+1}-\frac{f(1)}{2}=\frac{1}{2}(n-1) n+\frac{3}{4}(n-1)=\frac{1}{4}(n-1)(2 n+3) \text {. }
$$

Substituting $f(1)=\frac{3}{2}$ and rearranging, we get
$$
f(n)=\frac{1}{4} n(n+1)(2 n+1) \text {. }
$$

Thus, the required function is $f(x)=\frac{1}{4} x(x+1)(2 x+1)$ for $x \in \mathbb{N}$.
It is easy to verify that $f(x)$ satisfies the original functional equation.

In a circumference with center $ O$ we draw two equal chord $ AB\equal{}CD$ and if $ AB \cap CD \equal{}L$ then $ AL>BL$ and $ DL>CL$

meta.gold_solution:
1. **Given:**
   - Two equal chords \( AB \) and \( CD \) in a circle with center \( O \).
   - \( AB \cap CD = L \) such that \( AL > BL \) and \( DL > CL \).
   - Points \( M \in AL \) and \( N \in DL \) such that \( \angle ALC = 2 \angle MON \).

2. **Objective:**
   - Prove that the chord determined by extending \( MN \) has the same length as both \( AB \) and \( CD \).

3. **Initial Setup:**
   - Let \( OM \) and \( ON \) intersect the line segment \( BC \) at points \( E \) and \( F \) respectively.

4. **Properties of the Chords and Projections:**
   - Since \( AB = CD \) and \( ABCD \) is cyclic, \( ABCD \) forms an isosceles trapezoid.
   - \( BL = CL \implies AL = DL \).
   - \( \angle BAD = \angle CDA = \angle DCB = \angle ABC \).

5. **Perpendicular Projections:**
   - \( OP \perp AB \) and \( OQ \perp CD \) imply \( AP = PB \) and \( QD = QC \).
   - \( AL = DL \) implies \( PL = QL \).

6. **Angles and Parallel Lines:**
   - \( \angle LPQ = \angle LQP = \angle ABC \) implies \( BC \parallel PQ \).
   - \( OL \perp PQ \) implies \( \angle MOP = \angle NOL \).
   - \( OL \perp BC \) implies \( \angle DCB = \angle NOE \).

7. **Cyclic Quadrilaterals:**
   - \( CENO \) is cyclic, and similarly, \( BFMO \) is cyclic.
   - Since \( OB = OC \), \( \angle OBC = \angle OCB \) implies \( \angle OCN = \angle OBM = \angle OEN = \angle OFM \).

8. **Cyclic Properties and Angles:**
   - \( MEFN \) is cyclic, implying \( \angle OFE = \angle OMN \).
   - \( \angle MOP = \angle NOL \) implies \( \angle OFE = \angle OMP \).

9. **Chord Lengths:**
   - \( \angle OMP = \angle OMN \) implies \( \angle OMX = \angle OMB \) if \( MN \) cuts the circle at \( X \) and \( Y \).
   - Let the angle bisector of \( \angle BOX \) cut \( XM \) at \( K \), and assume \( K \) lies between \( X \) and \( M \).

10. **Contradiction and Conclusion:**
    - \( \angle OMX + \angle KOM = \angle OKX = \angle OKB \) implies \( \angle OKB > \angle OMX = \angle OMB \), which is a contradiction.

question: A positive integer is called simple if its ordinary decimal representation consists entirely of zeroes and ones. Find the least positive integer $k$ such that each positive integer $n$ can be written as $n = a_1 \pm a_2 \pm a_3 \pm \cdots \pm a_k$ where $a_1, \dots , a_k$ are simple.

meta.gold_solution:
To determine if \( k = 9 \) is the least positive integer such that each positive integer \( n \) can be written as \( n = a_1 \pm a_2 \pm a_3 \pm \cdots \pm a_k \) where \( a_1, \dots , a_k \) are simple, we need to explore the construction and verify if a smaller \( k \) can work.

1. **Understanding the Construction for \( k = 9 \)**:
   - Given a positive integer \( n \), we can represent it in its decimal form.
   - Construct nine simple integers \( s_1, s_2, \ldots, s_9 \) such that the \( k \)-th digit in \( s_i \) equals \( 1 \) if and only if the \( k \)-th digit of \( n \) is \( i \) or larger.
   - This ensures that each digit of \( n \) is represented by a combination of the digits of \( s_1, s_2, \ldots, s_9 \).

2. **Example for Clarity**:
   - Consider \( n = 432 \).
   - The simple integers \( s_1, s_2, \ldots, s_9 \) would be:
     \[
     s_1 = 111, \quad s_2 = 111, \quad s_3 = 111, \quad s_4 = 100, \quad s_5 = 000, \quad s_6 = 000, \quad s_7 = 000, \quad s_8 = 000, \quad s_9 = 000
     \]
   - Here, \( s_1, s_2, s_3 \) have all digits as 1 because the digits of \( n \) (4, 3, 2) are all greater than or equal to 1, 2, and 3 respectively. \( s_4 \) has a 1 in the first digit because the first digit of \( n \) is 4, which is greater than or equal to 4.

3. **Checking if \( k = 8 \) or Smaller Can Work**:
   - Suppose \( k = 8 \). We need to check if every positive integer \( n \) can be represented using 8 simple integers.
   - Consider a number \( n \) with a digit 9. To represent this digit, we need at least 9 simple integers because each simple integer can only contribute a 1 or 0 in each digit place.
   - Therefore, \( k = 8 \) is insufficient to represent a digit 9 in \( n \).

4. **Conclusion**:
   - Since \( k = 8 \) is insufficient and \( k = 9 \) works for any positive integer \( n \), \( k = 9 \) is indeed the least positive integer that satisfies the condition.

The final answer is \( \boxed{ k = 9 } \).

Shapovalov A.V.

Each face of a cube $6 \times 6 \times 6$ is divided into $1 \times 1$ cells. The cube is covered with $2 \times 2$ squares such that each square covers exactly four cells, no squares overlap, and each cell is covered by the same number of squares. What is the maximum value that this identical number can take? (Squares can be bent over the edge.)

meta.gold_solution:
Evaluation. A cell in the corner of a face can be covered in three ways (entirely within the face, with a fold over one edge of the corner, with a fold over the other edge of the corner). This means that each cell is covered by no more than three squares.

Example. Consider the usual covering of a cube with squares, where each face is covered by nine squares. From the usual covering, we can obtain a rotated one: leave two opposite faces untouched, and on the other four faces, shift all the squares in a ring by one cell. Since a pair of opposite faces can be chosen in three ways, there will be exactly three rotated coverings.

We will show that no two squares on coverings rotated differently coincide. Indeed, consider one face. On the diagram, the centers of the squares covering it are marked: with crosses if this face was not shifted, with black and white dots - if it was shifted in one or the other direction. It is clear that no centers, and therefore no squares, coincide.

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2024_05_06_b3ab7e582e0ed8c4b2bbg-22.jpg?height=449&width=443&top_left_y=1656&top_left_x=802)

## Answer

3.

question: 26th Putnam 1965 Problem B4 Define f n : R → R by f n (x) = (nC0 + nC2 x + nC4 x 2 + ... ) / (nC1 + nC3 x + nC5 x 2 + ... ), where nCm is the binomial coefficient. Find a formula for f n+1 (x) in terms of f n (x) and x, and determine lim n→∞ f n (x) for all real x.

meta.gold_solution: It is almost obvious that f n+1 = (f n + x)/(f n + 1) (*). So if f n (x) tends to a limit k(x), then k(x) = ( k(x) + x) /( k(x) + 1), and hence k(x) = √x. Obviously, f n (0) = 1/n, so k(0) = 0. We notice also that f n (x) = (√x) N/D, where N = (1 + √x) n + (1 - √x) n and D = (1 + √x) n - (1 - √x) n . Suppose 0  1, put y = (√x - 1)/(1 + √x) and we again get k(x) = √x. It is clear from (*), that for x < 0, f n (x) does not tend to a limit. 26th Putnam 1965 © John Scholes jscholes@kalva.demon.co.uk 25 Jan 2002

question: The distance of a light point from a sphere is equal to three times the radius of the sphere. How does the illuminated part of the sphere's surface relate to the lateral surface of the light cone?

meta.gold_solution:
Let the radius of the sphere be $r$, the radius of the base of the cone be $x$, the slant height of the cone be $l$, and the height of the illuminated spherical cap be $r-y$. The lateral surface area of the cone is $P=x \pi l$, and the surface area of the illuminated spherical cap is $F=2 r \pi(r-y)$. The values of $x$ and $y$ are determined as follows:

$$
x^{2}=r^{2}-y^{2}=(4 r-y) y
$$

from which

$$
y=\frac{r}{4} \text { and } x=\frac{r}{4} \sqrt{15}
$$

and since $l=4 x$, therefore $l=r \sqrt{15}$. Using these data:

$$
P=\frac{15 r^{2} \pi}{4} \text { and } F=\frac{3 r^{2} \pi}{2}
$$

why is it that:

$$
F: P=2: 5
$$

(István Bella.)

The problem was also solved by: Barna D., Döme B., Freibauer E., Juvancz I., Koós A., Krausz B., Gy. Krisztián, Gy. Lukhaub, R. Obláth, J. Prohászka, G. Sasvári, J. Weisz.

question: Determine the number of $ 8$-tuples of nonnegative integers $ (a_1,a_2,a_3,a_4,b_1,b_2,b_3,b_4)$ satisfying $ 0\le a_k\le k$, for each $ k \equal{} 1,2,3,4$, and $ a_1 \plus{} a_2 \plus{} a_3 \plus{} a_4 \plus{} 2b_1 \plus{} 3b_2 \plus{} 4b_3 \plus{} 5b_4 \equal{} 19$.

meta.gold_solution:
1. **Define new variables**: Let \( c_k = a_k + (k+1)b_k \). This transformation helps us simplify the problem by combining \( a_k \) and \( b_k \) into a single variable \( c_k \).

2. **Determine \( a_k \) and \( b_k \) from \( c_k \)**: Note that there is only one way to write \( c_k \) in the given form:
   \[
   b_k = \left\lfloor \frac{c_k}{k+1} \right\rfloor
   \]
   and
   \[
   a_k = c_k - (k+1) \left\lfloor \frac{c_k}{k+1} \right\rfloor.
   \]
   This means \( b_k \) is the number of complete times \( k+1 \) goes into \( c_k \), and \( a_k \) is the remainder of \( c_k \) upon division by \( k+1 \).

3. **Rewrite the original equation**: The original equation \( a_1 + a_2 + a_3 + a_4 + 2b_1 + 3b_2 + 4b_3 + 5b_4 = 19 \) can be rewritten using \( c_k \):
   \[
   c_1 + c_2 + c_3 + c_4 = 19.
   \]

4. **Count the number of solutions**: We need to find the number of nonnegative integer solutions to the equation \( c_1 + c_2 + c_3 + c_4 = 19 \). This is a classic "stars and bars" problem, where we distribute 19 indistinguishable stars (units) into 4 distinguishable bins (variables \( c_1, c_2, c_3, c_4 \)).

5. **Apply the stars and bars theorem**: The number of nonnegative integer solutions to \( c_1 + c_2 + c_3 + c_4 = 19 \) is given by:
   \[
   \binom{19 + 4 - 1}{4 - 1} = \binom{22}{3}.
   \]

6. **Calculate the binomial coefficient**:
   \[
   \binom{22}{3} = \frac{22 \times 21 \times 20}{3 \times 2 \times 1} = 1540.
   \]

Conclusion:
\[
\boxed{1540}
\]

question:
## Zadatak B-2.2.

Pravokutan trokut kojemu je hipotenuza trostruko dulja od jedne katete rotira oko hipotenuze. Odredite omjer obujma tako nastalog tijela i obujma tom tijelu opisane kugle.

meta.gold_solution:
## Rješenje.

Označimo li duljinu jedne katete s $x$, tada je duljina hipotenuze jednaka $3 x$, a duljina druge katete $\sqrt{9 x^{2}-x^{2}}=\sqrt{8 x^{2}}=2 \sqrt{2} x$.

Zarotiramo trokut oko hipotenuze i dobivenom tijelu opišemo kuglu. Na slici je prikazan poprečni presjek rotacijskog tijela i njemu opisane kugle.

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2024_05_30_ea3ef29009412d1e0d2bg-07.jpg?height=640&width=671&top_left_y=1719&top_left_x=196)

Dobiveno se tijelo sastoji od dva stošca kojima je baza zajednička, a polumjer baze je visina pravokutnog trokuta spuštena iz vrha pravoga kuta (na slici označena s $v$ ).

Izrazimo li površinu pravokutnog trokuta na dva načina:
$P=\frac{x \cdot 2 \sqrt{2} x}{2}$ i $P=\frac{3 x \cdot v}{2}$, dobivamo $\frac{x \cdot 2 \sqrt{2} x}{2}=\frac{3 x \cdot v}{2}$,

odakle slijedi $v=\frac{2 \sqrt{2}}{3} x$.

Zbroj duljina visina dvaju spojenih stožaca jednak je duljini hipotenuze $3 x$, te ih možemo označiti s $x_{1}$ i $\left(3 x-x_{1}\right)$.

Obujam dobivenog tijela je:

$$
\begin{aligned}
V_{t} & =\frac{v^{2} \pi x_{1}}{3}+\frac{v^{2} \pi\left(3 x-x_{1}\right)}{3} \\
V_{t} & =\frac{v^{2} \pi x_{1}+v^{2} \pi \cdot 3 x-v^{2} \pi x_{1}}{3} \\
V_{t} & =v^{2} \pi x
\end{aligned}
$$

Uvrštavanjem $v=\frac{2 \sqrt{2}}{3} x$ dobivamo $V_{t}=\left(\frac{2 \sqrt{2}}{3} x\right)^{2} \pi x=\frac{8 x^{3} \pi}{9}$.

Središte kugle opisane nastalom tijelu nalazi se u polovištu hipotenuze, pa je polumjer kugle $R=\frac{3 x}{2}$, a obujam kugle

$$
V_{\text {kugle }}=\frac{4}{3}\left(\frac{3 x}{2}\right)^{3} \pi=\frac{9 x^{3} \pi}{2}
$$

Omjer obujma nastalog tijela i obujma njemu opisane kugle jednak je

$$
\frac{V_{t}}{V_{\text {kugle }}}=\frac{\frac{8 x^{3} \pi}{9}}{\frac{9 x^{3} \pi}{2}}=\frac{16}{81}
$$

question: 60th Putnam 1999 Problem B1 The triangle ABC has AC = 1, angle ACB = 90 o , and angle BAC = φ. D is the point between A and B such that AD = 1. E is the point between B and C such that angle EDC = φ. The perpendicular to BC at E meets AB at F. Find lim φ→0 EF.

meta.gold_solution: Considering ACD, angle ACD = angle ADC = 90 o - φ/2. Hence angle DCE = φ/2. So, using the sine rule on triangle CDE: CE/DE = sin φ/sin(φ/2) which tends to 2. Angle EBD = 90 o - φ, angle EDB = 90 o - φ/2. So DE/EB = cos φ/cos(φ/2) which tends to 1. Hence EB/CE tends to 1/2 or EB/BC tends to 1/3. But EF/AC = EB/BC, so EF tends to AC/3 = 1/3. 60th Putnam 1999 © John Scholes jscholes@kalva.demon.co.uk 14 Dec 1999

question:
In a container with a heat-conductive wall and a piston, there is $V_{0}=1 \mathrm{~m}^{3}$ volume, $10^{5} \mathrm{~Pa}$ pressure, and $300 \mathrm{~K}$ temperature nitrogen. We perform two experiments with the gas.

a) We change the state of the gas in such a way that the ratio $\Delta p / \Delta V$ is kept at a constant value $a_{1}$. We observe that no matter whether we increase or decrease the volume of the nitrogen relative to $V_{0}$, the nitrogen always condenses.

b) In the second case, we also ensure that $\Delta p / \Delta V=a_{2}$ remains constant. Here, we observe that no matter whether we decrease or increase the volume of the gas relative to $V_{0}$, the system releases heat to its environment.

Determine the values of $a_{1}$ and $a_{2}$!

meta.gold_solution:
I. solution.
a) $\mathrm{A} \frac{\Delta_{p}}{\Delta_{V}}=a_{1}=$ the state condition means that during such a process, the state of the system, when plotted on a $p-V$ diagram, results in a straight line.

$$
\frac{p-p_{0}}{V-V_{0}}=a_{1}
$$

from this:

$$
p=a_{1} V+\left(-a_{1} V_{0}+p_{0}\right)
$$

on the other hand:

$$
p V=N k T
$$

thus the temperature during the process is

$$
T(V)=\frac{T_{0}}{p_{0} V_{0}} p V=\frac{T_{0}}{p_{0} V_{0}}\left[a_{1} V^{2}+\left(-a_{1} V_{0}+p_{0}\right) V\right]
$$

From the fact that this function has a maximum at $V_{0}$ (by differentiation or by completing the square), we get

$$
a_{1}=-\frac{p_{0}}{V_{0}}=-10^{5} \mathrm{~Pa} / \mathrm{m}^{3}
$$

b) During the second process

$$
\frac{p-p_{0}}{V-V_{0}}=a_{2}, \text { so } p=a_{2} V+p_{0}-a_{2} V_{0}
$$

Applying the first law of thermodynamics, the heat absorbed during the process is:

$$
Q=\Delta E+W^{\prime}=\frac{5}{2} N k\left(T-T_{0}\right)+\frac{\left(V-V_{0}\right)\left(p+p_{0}\right)}{2}
$$

where we used the fact that the heat capacity of diatomic nitrogen gas is $\frac{5}{2} N k, W^{\prime}$ is the area of the trapezoid under the $p-V$ state curve. Substituting $T=\frac{p V T_{0}}{p_{0} V_{0}} t$ and expressing $p$ in terms of $V$:

$$
Q(V)=3 a_{2} V^{2}+V\left(\frac{7}{2} p_{0}-\frac{7}{2} a_{2} V_{0}\right)-\frac{7}{2} p_{0} V_{0}+\frac{1}{2} a_{2} V_{0}^{2}
$$

The function $Q(V)$ must have a maximum at $V_{0}$, so

$$
a_{2}=\frac{7}{2} \frac{p_{0}}{V_{0}}=-1.4 \cdot 10^{5} \mathrm{~Pa} / \mathrm{m}^{3}
$$

Based on the work of Tamás Wiandt (Bonyhád, Petőfi S. Gymnasium, IV. grade)

II. solution. The problem can also be solved by using the following statements:

a) Higher isotherms define higher temperature states.

b) When moving from a higher adiabat to a lower adiabat (during any quasi-static process), the system releases heat.

From this, it is clear that to solve the problem, we need to determine the slope of the tangents at the given points. This can be done most simply by differentiation.

question:
A [i]cross [/i] is the figure composed of $6$ unit squares shown below (and any figure made of it by rotation).
[img]https://cdn.artofproblemsolving.com/attachments/6/0/6d4e0579d2e4c4fa67fd1219837576189ec9cb.png[/img]
Find the greatest number of crosses that can be cut from a $6 \times 11$ divided sheet of paper into unit squares (in such a way that each cross consists of six such squares).

meta.gold_solution:
1. **Understanding the Problem:**
   - We need to find the maximum number of crosses that can be cut from a \(6 \times 11\) grid of unit squares.
   - Each cross is composed of 6 unit squares.

2. **Analyzing the Cross:**
   - A cross consists of a central square and 4 arms extending from it, each arm being 1 unit square long.
   - The cross can be visualized as follows:
     ```
     . . . . .
     . . X . .
     . X X X .
     . . X . .
     . . . . .
     ```
   - The central square is denoted by \(C\).

3. **Placement Constraints:**
   - The central square \(C\) of the cross must be placed such that the arms do not extend beyond the boundary of the \(6 \times 11\) grid.
   - This means \(C\) must be at least 1 unit away from the boundary in all directions.

4. **Calculating the Valid Positions for \(C\):**
   - For a \(6 \times 11\) grid, the valid positions for \(C\) are:
     - Rows: 2 to 5 (4 possible rows)
     - Columns: 2 to 10 (9 possible columns)
   - Total valid positions for \(C\) = \(4 \times 9 = 36\).

5. **Maximizing the Number of Crosses:**
   - Each cross covers 6 unit squares.
   - The total number of unit squares in the grid is \(6 \times 11 = 66\).
   - The maximum number of crosses that can be cut is given by:
     \[
     \left\lfloor \frac{66}{6} \right\rfloor = 11
     \]
   - However, we need to ensure that the crosses do not overlap and fit within the grid.

6. **Considering Overlap and Boundary Constraints:**
   - Placing crosses without overlap and within the boundary constraints is more complex.
   - The solution provided suggests that the maximum number of crosses is 8, considering the boundary constraints and overlap.

7. **Verification:**
   - Let's verify the calculation:
     - The boundary tiles are those that cannot be the center \(C\) of any cross.
     - There are 30 such boundary tiles.
     - Each cross can cover at most 2 boundary tiles.
     - Thus, the number of crosses is:
       \[
       \left\lfloor \frac{66 - \frac{30}{2}}{6} \right\rfloor = \left\lfloor \frac{66 - 15}{6} \right\rfloor = \left\lfloor \frac{51}{6} \right\rfloor = 8
       \]

The final answer is \(\boxed{8}\)

question:
1. Replace each of the stars in the units place of the numbers in the expression

$$
\left|\frac{77777777777 *}{77777777777 *}-\frac{555555555554}{555555555559}\right|
$$

with some digit so that the expression takes on the smallest possible value.

meta.gold_solution:
SOLUTION. Let $x$ and $y$ be the digits we will add to the numerator and denominator of the first fraction, respectively. Since we will algebraically manipulate the entire expression in absolute value, for the sake of clearer notation, we introduce the designation $N=11111111110$. The individual numbers in the given expression can then be expressed as:

$$
\begin{aligned}
& 77777777777 x=7 N+x, \\
& 77777777777 y=7 N+y, \\
& 555555555554=5 N+4, \\
& 555555555559=5 N+9 .
\end{aligned}
$$

The expression under consideration can then be written and simplified as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}
& \left|\frac{7 N+x}{7 N+y}-\frac{5 N+4}{5 N+9}\right|=\frac{|(7 N+x)(5 N+9)-(5 N+4)(7 N+y)|}{(7 N+y)(5 N+9)}= \\
& =\frac{\left|\left(35 N^{2}+5 x N+63 N+9 x\right)-\left(35 N^{2}+5 y N+28 N+4 y\right)\right|}{(7 N+y)(5 N+9)}= \\
& =\frac{|5 \cdot(7-y+x) \cdot N+9 x-4 y|}{(7 N+y)(5 N+9)} .
\end{aligned}
$$

Let us also denote the numerator and denominator of the obtained fraction:

$$
C=|5 \cdot(7-y+x) \cdot N+9 x-4 y| \quad \text { and } \quad D=(7 N+y)(5 N+9) \text {. }
$$

If we substitute different pairs of digits for $x, y$, the denominator $D$ will take only ten different values in the range

$$
(7 N+0)(5 N+9) \leqq D \leqq(7 N+9)(5 N+9)
$$

Now let's see what large or small values the numerator $C$ will take. Since the number $9 x-4 y$ is at most two-digit, while the number $N$ is twelve-digit, the order of the numerator $C$ will depend on whether the factor $(7-y+x)$ is zero or not. Therefore, we will consider these two possibilities separately.

A. Case $7-y+x=0$. Then $y=x+7$ and the numerator $C$ is of the form

$$
C=|5 \cdot 0 \cdot N+(9 x-4 y)|=|9 x-4(x+7)|=|5 x-28| .
$$

Since the digit $y$ (equal to $x+7$) is at most 9, the digit $x$ is 0, 1, or 2, so the expression $|5 x-28|$ equals 28, 23, or 18. The smallest value of the numerator $C$ is thus 18 and is achieved only for $x=2$ and $y=9$. By a fortunate "coincidence," the denominator $D$ has its largest value for $y=9$, so

$$
\min \left\{\frac{C}{D}\right\}=\frac{18}{(7 N+9)(5 N+9)}
$$

B. Case $7-y+x \neq 0$. Let's show that the values of the numerator $C$ (and thus the values of the fraction $C / D$) are "enormous" in comparison to case A. From the inequality $7-y+x \neq 0$ it follows that $|7-y+x| \geqq 1$ (the number $7-y+x$ is an integer), so we have

$$
C=|5 \cdot(7-y+x) \cdot N+9 x-4 y| \geqq 5 \cdot|7-y+x| \cdot N-|9 x-4 y| \geqq 5 N-|9 x-4 y| .
$$

Since $x$ and $y$ are digits, it is clear that $|9 x-4 y| \leqq 81$. From the last estimate of $C$ and the maximum value of $D$, it follows that

$$
\frac{C}{D} \geqq \frac{5 N-81}{(7 N+9)(5 N+9)}
$$

The last fraction is "many times" larger than the fraction at the end of case A, because both fractions have the same denominator, while comparing the numerators clearly results in: $5 N-81 \gg 18$ (the inequality $5 N-81>18$ holds for values of $N \geq 20$).

Conclusion: We will add the digit $x=2$ to the numerator and the digit $y=9$ to the denominator.

question:
Compute the number of subsets $S$ of $\{0,1,\dots,14\}$ with the property that for each $n=0,1,\dots,
6$, either $n$ is in $S$ or both of $2n+1$ and $2n+2$ are in $S$.

[i]Proposed by Evan Chen[/i]

meta.gold_solution:
To solve the problem, we need to compute the number of subsets \( S \) of \( \{0, 1, \dots, 14\} \) such that for each \( n = 0, 1, \dots, 6 \), either \( n \) is in \( S \) or both \( 2n+1 \) and \( 2n+2 \) are in \( S \).

1. **Understanding the Condition:**
   - For each \( n \) in \( \{0, 1, \dots, 6\} \), either \( n \) is in \( S \) or both \( 2n+1 \) and \( 2n+2 \) are in \( S \).
   - This condition can be visualized using a binary tree structure where each node \( n \) has children \( 2n+1 \) and \( 2n+2 \).

2. **Recursive Formula:**
   - Let \( s_n \) be the number of subsets of \( \{0, 1, \dots, 2^n-2\} \) satisfying the given condition.
   - Consider the root node \( 0 \):
     - If \( 0 \) is in \( S \), then we can independently choose subsets for the subtrees rooted at \( 1 \) and \( 2 \). This gives \( s_{n-1}^2 \) possibilities.
     - If \( 0 \) is not in \( S \), then both \( 1 \) and \( 2 \) must be in \( S \). We then independently choose subsets for the subtrees rooted at \( 3, 4, 5, \) and \( 6 \). This gives \( s_{n-2}^4 \) possibilities.
   - Therefore, the recursive formula is:
     \[
     s_n = s_{n-1}^2 + s_{n-2}^4
     \]

3. **Base Cases:**
   - For \( n = 0 \), the set is empty, so \( s_0 = 1 \).
   - For \( n = 1 \), the set is \( \{0\} \). We can either include \( 0 \) or include both \( 1 \) and \( 2 \). Thus, \( s_1 = 2 \).

4. **Calculating \( s_2, s_3, \) and \( s_4 \):**
   - Using the recursive formula:
     \[
     s_2 = s_1^2 + s_0^4 = 2^2 + 1^4 = 4 + 1 = 5
     \]
     \[
     s_3 = s_2^2 + s_1^4 = 5^2 + 2^4 = 25 + 16 = 41
     \]
     \[
     s_4 = s_3^2 + s_2^4 = 41^2 + 5^4 = 1681 + 625 = 2306
     \]

Thus, the number of subsets \( S \) of \( \{0, 1, \dots, 14\} \) satisfying the given condition is \( \boxed{2306} \).

question:
Example 6 Solve the equation
\[
\begin{array}{l}
a^{4} \cdot \frac{(x-b)(x-c)}{(a-b)(a-c)}+b^{4} \cdot \frac{(x-c)(x-a)}{(b-c)} \\
+\epsilon^{4} \cdot \frac{(x-a)(x-b)}{(c-a)(c-b)}=x^{4} .
\end{array}
\]

meta.gold_solution:
Solution: It is easy to know from the definition that $x_{1}=a$ is a root of the original equation. Since $a, b, c$ in the original equation are cyclically symmetric, by the property of cyclically symmetric expressions, $x_{2}=b$ and $x_{3}=c$ are also roots of the original equation. Let $x_{4}$ be another root of the equation, then
$$
(x-a)(x-b)(x-c)\left(x-x_{4}\right)=0 \text {. }
$$

Expanding and rearranging, we get
$$
x^{4}-\left(a+b+c+x_{4}\right) x^{3}+\cdots=0 .
$$

Since the coefficient of $x^{3}$ in the original equation is 0, we have
$$
\begin{array}{l}
a+b+c+x_{4}=0 . \\

question: 9. (16 points) In the acute triangle $\triangle ABC$, $a, b, c$ are the sides opposite to $\angle A, \angle B, \angle C$ respectively, and $a, b, c$ form an arithmetic sequence, $\sin (A-C)=\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}$. Find $\sin (A+C)$.

$$
a+c=2 b \text {. }
$$

By the Law of Sines, we know
$$
\sin A+\sin C=2 \sin B \text {. }
$$

In the acute $\triangle A B C$, we have
$$
\begin{array}{l}
\sin (A-C)=\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2} \\
\Rightarrow \angle A-\angle C=\frac{\pi}{3} .
\end{array}
$$

Since $\angle A+\angle B+\angle C=\pi$, then $\angle A=\frac{2 \pi}{3}-\frac{\angle B}{2}, \angle C=\frac{\pi}{3}-\frac{\angle B}{2}$

question: Find all functions $f: N_0 \to N_0$, (where $N_0$ is the set of all non-negative integers) such that $f(f(n))=f(n)+1$ for all $n \in N_0$ and the minimum of the set $\{ f(0), f(1), f(2) \cdots \}$ is $1$.

meta.gold_solution:

   f(f(n)) = f(n) + 1 \quad \forall n \in \mathbb{N}_0
   \]

2. Let's denote \(m\) as the minimum value of the set \(\{ f(0), f(1), f(2), \ldots \}\). According to the problem, \(m = 1\). Therefore, there exists some \(k \in \mathbb{N}_0\) such that \(f(k) = 1\).

3. Consider \(f(f(k))\). By the given functional equation:
   \[
   f(f(k)) = f(k) + 1 = 1 + 1 = 2
   \]
   Thus, \(f(1) = 2\).

4. Next, consider \(f(f(1))\):
   \[
   f(f(1)) = f(1) + 1 = 2 + 1 = 3
   \]
   Thus, \(f(2) = 3\).

5. We can generalize this pattern. Suppose \(f(n) = n + 1\) for some \(n \in \mathbb{N}_0\). Then:
   \[
   f(f(n)) = f(n + 1)
   \]
   By the functional equation:
   \[
   f(f(n)) = f(n) + 1 = (n + 1) + 1 = n + 2
   \]
   Therefore, \(f(n + 1) = n + 2\).

6. By induction, we can show that \(f(n) = n + 1\) for all \(n \in \mathbb{N}_0\):
   - Base case: For \(n = 0\), we have \(f(0) = 1\), which satisfies the condition.
   - Inductive step: Assume \(f(k) = k + 1\) for some \(k \in \mathbb{N}_0\). Then:
     \[
     f(k + 1) = (k + 1) + 1 = k + 2
     \]
     Thus, by induction, \(f(n) = n + 1\) for all \(n \in \mathbb{N}_0\).

7. Finally, we verify that \(f(n) = n + 1\) satisfies the original functional equation:
   \[
   f(f(n)) = f(n + 1) = (n + 1) + 1 = n + 2
   \]
   and
   \[
   f(n) + 1 = (n + 1) + 1 = n + 2
   \]
   Both sides are equal, confirming that \(f(n) = n + 1\) is a solution.

Conclusion:
\[
\boxed{f(n) = n + 1}
\]

question: Example 5 Let $n \geqslant 3$ be a positive integer, and $a_{1}, a_{2}, \cdots, a_{n}$ be any $n$ distinct real numbers with a positive sum. meta.gold_solution:
Analysis and Solution: Consider the worst-case scenario: for $k=1,2, \cdots, n, b_{1}+b_{2}+\cdots+b_{k}>0$ is difficult to satisfy. This only requires that the number of negative numbers in $a_{1}, a_{2}, \cdots, a_{n}$ is as many as possible. Let $a_{2}, \cdots, a_{n}$ all be negative, and $a_{1}=-a_{2}-\cdots-a_{n}+1$. At this point, any good permutation $\left(b_{1}, b_{2}, \cdots, b_{n}\right)$ must have $b_{1}=a_{1}$, and $b_{2}, \cdots, b_{n}$ can be any permutation of $a_{2}, \cdots, a_{n}$. Therefore, there are $(n-1)!$ good permutations in this case.

Next, we prove that there are at least $(n-1)!$ good permutations. Note that $(n-1)!$ is the number of different circular permutations of $a_{1}, a_{2}, \cdots, a_{n}$. We first prove that each circular permutation corresponds to a good permutation. For convenience, we call the first term of a good permutation a good number. We only need to prove that each circular permutation must contain a good number.

Method 1: Induction on $n$. When $n=1$, the conclusion is obviously true. Assume that for all $n$, the conclusion holds. For $n+1$, since the sum of all numbers is positive, there is at least one positive number. Group each positive number and the next positive number in the clockwise direction, along with all the numbers between them, into one group. Each group has at least one number, and at least one group has at least two numbers (since not all numbers are positive), so there are at most $k-1$ groups. Summing the numbers in each group, we get fewer than $k$ sums. Write these sums in the order of their groups on the circle. Since the total sum of these sums is positive, by the induction hypothesis, there is a sum that is a good number. Consider the positive number in the group corresponding to this sum; this number is a good number in the entire circular permutation. By the principle of induction, the conclusion holds.

Method 2: Using the extremal principle. For any circular permutation $\left(b_{1}, b_{2}, \cdots, b_{n}\right)$, consider all partial sums starting with $b_{i}$: $b_{i}+b_{i+1}+\cdots+b_{i+t}$, where indices greater than $n$ are taken modulo $n$. For all $i=1,2, \cdots, n$ and all $t=0,1,2, \cdots, n-1$, there must be a smallest partial sum $b_{i}+b_{i+1}+\cdots+b_{i+c}$. Since there is at least one non-positive number, $b_{i}+b_{i+1}+\cdots+b_{i+t} \leqslant 0$. Among all such smallest sums, let the one with the largest number of terms $t+1$ be $b_{i}+b_{i+1}+\cdots+b_{i+t}$. We prove that $b_{i+t+1}$ is a good number.

Indeed, if there exists a positive integer $k$ such that $b_{i+t+1}+b_{i+t+2}+\cdots+b_{i+t+k} \leqslant 0$, then $\left(b_{i}+b_{i+1}+\cdots+b_{i+t}\right)+\left(b_{i+t+1}+b_{i+t+2}+\cdots+b_{i+t+k}\right) \leqslant b_{i}+b_{i+1}+\cdots+b_{i+t}$, which contradicts the fact that $b_{i}+b_{i+1}+\cdots+b_{i+t}$ is the smallest and has the most terms.

Since there are $(n-1)!$ circular permutations, and each circular permutation corresponds to at least one good permutation, and different circular permutations correspond to different good permutations, there are at least $(n-1)!$ good permutations.

In conclusion, the minimum value is $(n-1)!$.
